editorial.headline: Karaoke Facilities: Open Nationally, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Providing karaoke venues is nationally open to PMA at every listed scale, yet Bali’s permanent risk-based moratorium prevents PMA registration on the island.
editorial.body:
For a foreign investor, the decisive fact comes first: activity code 93292 cannot be registered as PMA in Bali today. That does not erase its national standing; it marks the difference between a nationwide investment classification and a province-wide registration restriction. Nationally, the activity is open to PMA and carries a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In Bali, it is marked as blocked because of its risk class. The national ceiling is therefore not a Bali authorisation: the activity may be nationally open while a PMA registration on the island remains unavailable.

The underlying business is the provision of a place and facilities for karaoke as the principal undertaking. That focus matters: the venue and karaoke facilities form the activity’s core. Food and beverage service may be provided alongside it, but the record describes that as an addition, not the defining business. The code is available at micro, small, medium and large scales. It is consequently framed to accommodate operations at each of those listed scales, without changing the essential description of a karaoke venue business.

Bali’s restriction rests on the risk treatment recorded for the large scale: every scope is assessed in OSS as Low or Medium-Low risk. Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium blocks all KBLI with Low or Medium-Low risk for PMA. The record consequently identifies the activity as blocked in Bali under the risk-class status. This is not a different Bali foreign-ownership percentage; it is a bar on the PMA registration itself. The cited provincial basis is the Governor’s letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP, and the record dates the moratorium to May 2026.

For founders, the disciplined reading is simple. The national record says the activity is open to PMA, and 100% is the national foreign-ownership ceiling. The Bali record says a PMA registration cannot be made there because the large-scale OSS risk classification falls within the province’s permanent prohibition. Those statements are not competing answers: they describe two different levels of rule. Any plan built around Bali must treat the island restriction as decisive, rather than treating national openness as a substitute for local registration availability.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness is not a Bali authorisation: the island’s PMA registration block is decisive.
